And Leo of Byzantium in the Boeotica, cited by Plutarch in the book On Rivers, says of the boy Cythaeron: Ὁ δὲ ὄφις, τοῖς κόλποις περισφίγξας, αὐτὸν ἀνεῖλεν· [Ho de ophis, tois kolpois perisphingxas, auton aneilen;] The serpent, having bound him tight in its coils, killed him. And Cicero, on Roscius, in the first book On Divination: At night, by the light of a lamp set beside him, the nurse, aroused, noticed the boy sleeping, encircled in the embrace of a serpent. And in the second book: About Roscius himself it may indeed be false that a snake was coiled around him. To this belongs the passage in Aelian's History, book 6, chapter 21, where the dragon that fights the elephant, τῷ τραχήλῳ περιερπόσας, θείνων τῷ οὐραίῳ μέρει, καὶ σφίγγων θατέρῳ, ἀπάγχει τὸ θηρίον ἀήθει βρόχῳ, καὶ καινῷ [tō trachēlō perierposas, theinōn tō ouraiō merei, kai sphingōn naterō, apanchei to thērion aēthei brochō, kai kainō], having crept around its neck, beating it with the tail end, and [col. 371] constricting it with the other, strangles the beast with a new and unaccustomed noose. And in the description of the caduceus in Macrobius, Saturnalia, book 1, chapter 19: [III, 142] These dragons are bound together at the middle of their coils by the knot they call the knot of Hercules.

There follows the judgment of the barbarians on this incident: And when the barbarians saw the beast hanging from his hand, they said to one another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though saved from the sea, justice does not allow to live.” The barbarians, that is, the Melitans. For Paul was then on the island of Melite, and the Melitans were counted as barbarians because most of the inhabitants of that island were neither Greeks nor Romans, but Φοινίκων, ἢ Καρχηδονίων ἄποικοι [Phoinikōn, ē Karchēdoniōn apoikoi], colonists of the Phoenicians or of the Carthaginians, as we have proved elsewhere from Scylax, Diodorus and Stephanus. Accordingly, in the First Punic War the Roman consul Atilius, in a naval expedition against the Carthaginians, ranged over and laid waste Lipara and Melita, famous islands of Sicily, as Orosius relates in book 4, chapter 8. And in the Second Punic War, T. Sempronius crossed from Lilybaeum to the island of Melita, which was held by the Carthaginians. On his arrival Hamilcar, son of Gisgo, commander of the garrison, with a little under two thousand soldiers, and the town on the island were surrendered to him. So Livy, Decade 3, book 1. And we have shown that the name Melite itself is Punic. The Melitans, then, were part of the Barbarians, like the other Punic peoples in Africa, from whom the region itself was at length named Barbaria. These, then, when they saw κρεμάμενον τὸ θηρίον [kremamenon to thērion], the beast hanging, that is, the viper, from the hand of Paul, etc. For θηρίον [thērion] signifies not only a beast in general but also a serpent, or a venomous beast. Thus Sirach. XII, 17. Τίς ἐλεήσει ἐπαοιδὸν ὀφιόδηκτον, καὶ πάντας τοὺς προσάγοντας θηρίοις; [Tis eleēsei epaoidon ophiodēkton, kai pantas tous prosagontas thēriois?] Who will pity a charmer bitten by a serpent, or any of those who approach beasts? supply venomous, that is, vipers or serpents. Dioscorides, book 1, the chapter On the chaste-tree: Τὰ φύλλα ὑποθυμιώμενά τε καὶ ὑποστρωννύμενα θηρία διώκει· [Ta phylla hypothymiōmena te kai hypostrōnnymena thēria diōkei;] which Pliny renders thus in book 24, chapter 9: By fumigation too, or when strewn beneath, they (the leaves) drive away venomous creatures. Hence throughout the books of the physicians θηριόδηγμα [thēriodēgma] and θηριόδηκτος [thēriodēktos] are used of one who has been bitten by a serpent, and θηριακὰ φάρμακα [thēriaka pharmaka] of remedies that help against venomous creatures. Of the same kind is the fact that for Josephus, Antiquities, book 2, chapter 5, Ethiopia is a land θηριοτρόφος [thēriotrophos], because it nourishes many serpents. And in Galen the Marsi are θηριοτρόφοι [thēriotrophoi], because they feed on serpents. And in Dionysius of Halicarnassus the letter Σῖγμα [Sigma] is θηριώδης [thēriōdēs], because it imitates the hissing of serpents. So too the same word חיה is for the Hebrews any wild beast, and for the Arabs a serpent. And among the Chaldeans the words חיוא and חויא differ little: the former means beast in general, the latter serpent. Thus in Luke, then, τὸ θηρίον [to thērion] is a serpent, and indeed a viper; and when the barbarians saw it hanging from the hand of Paul, to which it had fastened itself, they concluded that he was a murderer, that is, guilty either of homicide or of some other grave crime. The species stands for the genus. By the same figure one of the Furies is called Τισιφόνη [Tisiphonē], ἀπὸ τοῦ τίειν τοὺς φόνους [apo tou tiein tous phonous]; for she was believed to be the avenger not of homicide alone but of other crimes too. [III, 143] And this was the barbarians' reason for passing so barbarous a judgment on a holy man: they saw him, scarcely escaped from one evil, presently fall into another, as though ἡ Δίκη [hē Dikē] would not allow him to live. Ἡ δίκη [Hē dikē], that is, Justice, a goddess; for so the ancients called her. Hesiod, in the Works, verse 254:

Ἡ δέ τε παρθένος ἐστὶ Δίκη, Διὸς ἐκγεγαυῖα, Κυδνή τ᾽, αἰδοίη τε Θεοῖς, οἳ Ὄλυμπον ἔχουσιν, Καί ῥ᾽ ὁπότ᾽ ἄν τίς μιν βλάπτῃ σκολιῶς ὀνοτάζων, Αὐτίκα παρ᾽ Διῒ πατρὶ καθεζομένη Κρονίωνι, Γηρύετ᾽ ἀνθρώπων ἄδικον νόον, etc. [Hē de te parthenos esti Dikē, Dios ekgegauia, Kydnē t', aidoiē te Theois, hoi Olympon echousin, Kai r' hopot' an tis min blaptē skoliōs onotazōn, Autika par' Dii patri kathezomenē Kroniōni, Gēryet' anthrōpōn adikon noon]
